About: Stopping Distance ∝ Speed²

Source

Topic
Equations of motion for uniform acceleration (kinematics, one dimension).
Simulation
Braking car — stopping distance vs. initial speed with stacked comparison bars.
Concept
Doubling the speed doubles the stopping time but quadruples the stopping distance: distance is quadratic in speed (v² = u² − 2as, a = deceleration).
Serves
Kinematics of uniformly accelerated motion; NCERT Class 11 Ch. 3.
Inquiry
Predict the stopping distance at 20 m/s after observing 10 m/s; commit before running.
Misconception
Stopping distance is proportional to speed. It is proportional to the square of the speed.

Stopping Distance ∝ Speed²
✦Teach me

Guided Inquiry

Step 1 · A baseline run

The car starts at u = 10 m/s and brakes with a = 5 m/s². Press ▶ Play and watch where it stops. The coloured bar left on the road spans where it braked from to where it ended. Read that distance off the road.

When it has stopped, tap Next →.

Step 2 · Predict: double the speed

Now the initial speed will be u = 20 m/s, the deceleration unchanged at 5 m/s². How far will the car travel before stopping?

Step 3 · Watch it stop

Press ▶ Play. The new bar stacks above the previous one on the same distance scale. Compare the lengths directly.

Notice the two readouts on the canvas: the stopping time only doubles (2 s → 4 s) while the stopping distance quadruples (10 m → 40 m). Same scene, both facts.

Step 4 · One more — u = 30 m/s

Predict in your head: 30 m/s is 3× the original speed, so the stopping distance should be 9× — around 90 m. Press ▶ Play and check.

You now have three stacked bars at 10, 20, 30 m/s. Their lengths are in the ratio 1 : 4 : 9 — the squares of the speeds.

Step 5 · The takeaway

From v² = u² − 2as (a is the magnitude of the braking deceleration) with v = 0 (car at rest):

d = u² / (2a)

Stopping distance is quadratic in speed. Stopping time (t = u/a) is only linear. Confusing the two is the standard error. Now play freely — drag initial speed and the deceleration to build up more bars.

The Physics

Equations of Motion for Uniform Acceleration · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A car brakes to a stop at a steady rate, and the sim leaves a bar on the road for every run so you can compare how far each one went. It lets you measure a road-safety rule instead of just being told it.

What you'll learn

  • How a braking car's stopping distance and stopping time depend on its starting speed u and its braking deceleration a.
  • How to turn a pair of braking numbers into a distance in metres and a time in seconds.
  • Where the equation v² = u² − 2as comes from, and what it says about a car that ends at rest.
The car brakes from speed u at a steady deceleration a until it stops. d is the distance it covers.

What's on screen

  • Road and car: a side view with a metre scale, and a braking starts mark at 0 m.
  • Stacked bars: one bar per run, from the start mark to where the car stopped, labelled u = … m/s → … m. The sim keeps the last three runs.
  • d and t box (top right): the stopping distance and time for the current u and a.
  • v label above the moving car: its speed right now.
See itRun the car from 10 m/s with a = 5 m/s². Watch for: the car stopping, and a bar marking the road from the start mark to where it ended.

03

Stopping distance grows as the square of the speed

At a fixed braking deceleration a, the stopping distance is

d = u² / (2a)
Distance depends on u², not on u.

So doubling u multiplies d by 2² = 4, and tripling it multiplies d by 3² = 9. With a = 5 m/s² the sim gives:

ustopping distance dcompared with 10 m/s
10 m/s10 m1×
20 m/s40 m4×
30 m/s90 m9×

The bars on the road keep this ratio because they all use the same metres-to-pixels scale.

See itAdd a 20 m/s run beside a 10 m/s run. Watch for: the second bar growing to 4 times the length of the first (10 m and 40 m).
04

Stopping time grows only in proportion to speed

Steady braking removes a fixed amount of speed every second, a metres per second each second. So the time to reach zero is

t = u / a
Time depends on u, not on u².
  • Doubling u doubles t: 2 s at 10 m/s becomes 4 s at 20 m/s.
  • Distance quadruples while time doubles because a faster car also moves faster during every second of the longer stop.
  • The d and t box shows both numbers for the current u and a.
See itRun 30 m/s after 10 and 20 m/s. Watch for: the box at the top right reading d = 90.00 m and t = 6.00 s: three times the time, nine times the distance.
05

Where d = u²/(2a) comes from

For steady motion, v² = u² − 2as, with a the size of the deceleration and s the distance covered. The car ends at rest, so v = 0 at s = d. That gives 0 = u² − 2ad, and d = u²/(2a).

Speed against time while braking. The area under the line is the distance.

The area is the triangle ½ × base × height = ½ × (u/a) × u, which is u²/(2a) again. The car's average speed over the stop is u/2, and it keeps that average for a time u/a.

See itRun 20 m/s and read the v label above the car. Watch for: v falling by the same 5 m/s every second, 20.0 → 15.0 → 10.0 → 5.0 → 0.
06

Braking harder shortens the stop in proportion

The deceleration a sits in the denominator of both results, so at a fixed u:

  • Double a: d and t are both halved.
  • Halve a: d and t are both doubled.

From 20 m/s, a = 2 m/s² needs 100 m and 10 s, a = 5 m/s² needs 40 m and 4 s, and a = 10 m/s² needs 20 m and 2 s. The speed enters the distance twice (as u²), the braking only once (as 1/a). The panel below uses the sim's own sliders.

u a

These sliders move the sim too.

See itRun 20 m/s with a = 5 m/s², then with a = 10 m/s². Watch for: the second bar half as long as the first, labelled a = 10 m/s².
07

Where it matters

  • Road safety. A car's kinetic energy ½mu² also goes as u². Doubling the speed quadruples the braking distance and the energy that must be absorbed.
  • Reaction time. Before the brakes act, a driver covers u × (reaction time) at full speed. At 20 m/s and 1 s that is another 20 m on top of the 40 m braking distance, and unlike the braking part it grows only in proportion to u.
  • Grip sets a. A tyre can give a deceleration of about μg at most, where μ is the friction coefficient between tyre and road. Roughly 7 m/s² on a dry road and 4 m/s² on a wet one, so the same speed needs a longer stop in the rain.
  • Road design. Engineers use the stopping distance at the design speed to decide how far ahead a driver must be able to see.
08

Summary

In one line. A car braking at constant deceleration a from speed u comes to rest after a distance and a time that are both fixed by u and a.

Key points

  • v² = u² − 2as with v = 0 gives the stopping distance d = u²/(2a).
  • The stopping time is t = u/a.
  • Doubling u doubles t but quadruples d; doubling a halves both.

Common mix-ups

  • "Twice the speed, twice the stopping distance." That is true of the time. The distance goes as the square of the speed, so it quadruples.
  • "The car stopping for twice as long means it travels twice as far." It also moves faster throughout, so the average speed doubles as well: 2 × 2 = 4 times the distance.
  • "a is negative, so d comes out negative." Here a is the size of the deceleration. The minus sign is already written in v² = u² − 2as, so d is positive.

Things to try on your own

  • With a = 5 m/s², run u = 10, 20 and 30 m/s, then divide each distance by u² and compare the three results.
  • Find two different pairs of u and a that both stop in 20 m, for example one with a = 10 m/s².
  • Set u = 40 m/s and find the smallest a that stops the car within 100 m.
